claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations.
A machine-learning framework using microstructure-informed descriptors can predict Young’s modulus for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
A machine-learning framework using microstructure-informed descriptors can predict yield strength for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
A machine-learning framework using microstructure-informed descriptors can predict toughness for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
Adding microstructural descriptors to machine learning will make the three property predictions more accurate than conventional CALPHAD or ab initio methods.
The integrated framework will provide more rapid predictions than conventional CALPHAD or ab initio methods.
Phase-boundary and chemical-fluctuation metrics can serve as informative microstructural descriptors for the proposed mechanical-property model.
Multilevel chemical fluctuations and resulting phase heterogeneity link processing conditions to mechanical performance in HfNbTiVAl10.
Combining thermophysical data, CALPHAD outputs, and microstructure observations allows the model to capture interrelationships governing elasticity, yielding, and fracture.
The integrated framework will improve prediction accuracy by approximately 10–15%.
The integrated framework will reduce computational time by at least an order of magnitude.
Ab initio methods are time-consuming for high-throughput alloy prediction, and CALPHAD can require significant computational resources.
Prior computational approaches generally do not capture complex interrelationships among multiple descriptors and thermomechanical properties.
The proposed method may become unreliable when its training data do not represent the relevant range of microstructural variation.
Processing-induced grain coarsening or nonuniform phase distributions outside the calibration range may make the model unreliable.
Quantitative gains in accuracy and efficiency depend on the quality and representativeness of the training data.
The hypothesis is defined as falsified if MAPE exceeds 15% for any one of the three properties on a statistically significant number of blinded samples.
